children.value: This chapter summarises the latent-state model: its generative assumptions, its six free parameters, and the way the parameters are estimated and validated. It gives the defining equations only. Derivations, all constants and the complete update rules are in

The equations describe the model adopted on 11 October 2026: the six-parameter agent with a commitment gain of 3, estimated with a network trained on 100,000 simulations and the 54 summary features of
. The decision, the validation and the alternatives examined are documented in
. The participant results in this book come from run

The model is a two-state hidden Markov model with von Mises emissions on the circle of 32 slots. An agent filters the latent state trial by trial, tracks the attack directions with gated delta-rule updates, and converts its predictive distribution into an allocation of seven nets. Six parameters govern this process. Because the mapping from parameters to allocations has no closed-form likelihood, the parameters are estimated by amortized simulation-based inference: a neural network is trained once on simulated sessions and then returns the posterior distribution for each participant.

Precision weighting enters at three points by design, so that a higher value yields a narrower predictive distribution, a more concentrated allocation and faster direction learning. The three effects cannot be separated within this model.
Parameters are drawn from the priors, one of the 20 trial schedules is drawn at random, and the agent is run on it.
Each simulated session is reduced to a fixed vector of summary features. The same code computes the features of simulated and of participants’ sessions.

For each participant, 4,000 posterior samples are drawn conditional on the participant’s features. No further fitting takes place.

Before the parameters are interpreted, an amortized classifier compares the model with four alternatives (random allocation, two tracking models without latent states, and coverage of both state directions without state inference). The parameters are meant to be interpreted only for participants for whom the latent-state model has the highest posterior probability (
The summary features are not sufficient statistics. Whether they carry enough information about each parameter is an empirical question, which the recovery and calibration analyses answer.
) with 1,000 simulations, the rank distributions of all six parameters remain inside the simultaneous 95% band of the graphical test (
). Rank means and rank dispersions lie within 1.5 standard errors of their expected values.

Recovery is high for precision weighting and placement noise, good for belief momentum, cue sensitivity and the switch probability, and moderate for noise reactivity (table above). In the range of precision weighting that participants occupy, the recovery of noise reactivity is .86. Estimates of one parameter are nearly uncorrelated with the true values of the others (at most .21). Within posteriors, noise reactivity and belief momentum are negatively correlated (mean −.64).

For the 62 participants classified as the latent-state model, the fitted agent reproduces the differences between participants in the main behavioural summaries (rank correlation between observed and predicted values of .87 to .96 for net entropy, trial-to-trial shift, angular error, placement variability and defense rate). The observed value lies inside the central 95% predictive interval for 56% of all features and participants; the intervals are narrow, and most deviations are offsets below half a between-participant standard deviation. The largest offsets concern the variability of the trial-to-trial shift.

Placement noise is a general measure of placement variability.

Participants alternate between precise placements and discrete moves to the other state’s direction or to the location of a preceding oddball. The agent represents all off-target placements by a Gaussian shift, so that placement noise includes these moves, and the variability of the trial-to-trial shift is underestimated.

Among the directed models, only the latent-state model has placement noise and cue sensitivity. A comparison with matched action noise is outstanding, and the classifier for the adopted agent is being retrained.
Posterior samples are clipped to the prior bounds, and several participants have estimates of cue sensitivity, placement noise, noise reactivity and the switch probability close to a bound.
